The Heated Disk

Is space a fact or a choice?

Geometry is not true or false. It is convenient — and Poincaré built a toy world to prove it.

2 min read3 figures, each sourcedWhere it is contestedUpdated 15 September 2026

Imagine creatures on a heated disk whose rulers shrink as they near the cold rim. They would swear their finite disk was an infinite curved plane — and no experiment they could ever run would tell them otherwise.

If you keep one line

No measurement interprets itself: every observation arrives bundled with assumptions about the instruments.

ShareEmailXLinkedIn

Henri Poincaré's disk, from 'Science and Hypothesis' (1902), is one of philosophy's great gadgets. Temperature falls from centre to rim; everything — rulers, bodies, light paths — contracts identically as it cools. Inhabitants measuring their world would derive hyperbolic geometry: straight lines bent, the rim infinitely far away. We would say: flat disk, shrinking rulers. They would say: curved space, honest rulers. Both descriptions predict every observation. Which is true?

Poincaré's answer: the question is empty. Experiments never test geometry alone — they test geometry plus physics, bundled. You can keep Euclid forever by blaming your instruments, or keep your instruments honest and buy a stranger geometry. The choice is a convention, made on grounds of convenience, like choosing metres over feet. This landed at the end of geometry's great humbling: after two thousand years of trying to prove the parallel postulate, Lobachevsky, Bolyai and Riemann had shown that consistent alternatives exist, and Hilbert had shown Euclid was never even airtight.

Then physics called the bluff. In 1915 Einstein's general relativity described gravity as curved spacetime — and light bent past the sun in 1919 exactly as the curved description predicted. Reichenbach and the positivists argued this refuted conventionalism: pick the geometry that eliminates 'universal forces' and it is non-Euclidean, full stop. Others reply that Einstein did precisely what Poincaré prescribed (chose the package that made the total physics simplest) and that this vindicates the framing rather than refuting it.

The reason to keep the disk in your pocket has nothing to do with geometry. It is the cleanest demonstration that no measurement interprets itself: every observation reaches you bundled with assumptions about the instruments, and when a result surprises you, the bundle — not the world — is often what gave way. Duhem said it about physics, Quine about everything; Poincaré built the toy that makes it obvious.

01By the numbers

~2,000 yrsOf failed attempts to prove the parallel postulate, ending with Lobachevsky and Bolyai: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Nineteenth Century Geometry'; Wikipedia, 'Parallel postulate'
1902'Science and Hypothesis' first published — the disk, and the conventionalist thesis: Wikipedia, 'Science and Hypothesis'
1919Eclipse measurements match the curved-spacetime package, 29 May 1919: Wikipedia, 'Solar eclipse of May 29, 1919'

02How it happened

  1. 1829Lobachevsky publishes a consistent geometry without the parallel postulate; Bolyai independently follows.
  2. 1854Riemann's habilitation lecture generalises geometry to curved spaces of any dimension.
  3. 1899Hilbert's 'Grundlagen der Geometrie' shows Euclid's own axioms needed repair.
  4. 1902'Science and Hypothesis': the heated disk, and geometry as convention.
  5. 1915General relativity casts gravity as spacetime curvature.
  6. 1919Eddington's eclipse expedition measures starlight bending past the sun.

03Who did the work

Henri PoincaréThe last mathematician at home in every branch of the subject; built philosophy's best toy world as an aside.
Bernhard RiemannGeneralised geometry so thoroughly in one lecture that physics took sixty years to need it.
Hans ReichenbachTurned the conventionality question into a precise programme — and the standing argument about whether Einstein settled it.

04Where it is contested

Whether general relativity refutes Poincaré or enacts him is a live philosophy-of-physics fight a century on. Reichenbach's rule — define away universal forces, then geometry is empirical — is itself a convention, say the conventionalists. The literature has not settled; it has professionalised.

05What I changed my mind about

I once spent a week inside the disk with a ruler, computing how distances warp near the rim, and came out changed about something else entirely: I stopped saying 'the data show' without asking what instrument-assumptions were bundled into the showing. The disk is a machine for manufacturing that reflex.

06Go to the source

Science and HypothesisHenri Poincaré, 1902
Free, short chapters, and the source. The geometry chapters are the heart.
On the Hypotheses Which Lie at the Bases of GeometryBernhard Riemann, 1854, in W. K. Clifford's translation
The lecture that made curved space thinkable — readable even where the mathematics is not.
Nineteenth Century GeometryStanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy
The whole arc — parallel postulate to Poincaré — with the philosophy kept honest.
The Philosophy of Space and TimeHans Reichenbach
The strongest case that Einstein closed the question. Decide for yourself whether it begs it.
